**Stage 3 complete.** Plan at `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-07-sma-457-ci-integration-jobs.md` (commit `299b2b7`).

**7 tasks, 9 files** (1 created, 8 modified):

| Task | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| 1 | `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL` guard in `temporal_live.rs` — the never-green-by-skip fix |
| 2 | BuildKit cache mounts in the AgentCore Dockerfile |
| 3 | Overridable cold-start gate + loud NOTE + job summary in the check script |
| 4 | `integration.yml` scaffold + `temporal-it` |
| 5 | `agentcore-image` job |
| 6 | Five doc files |
| 7 | Full gate run, push, record measured CI figures |

Two things worth flagging about how the plan turned out:

**Local verification is much stronger than I assumed.** `protoc`, the `temporal` CLI, and `actionlint` are all installed here. So Task 1 runs the *entire* six-test Temporal suite against a real local dev server — including the exact `operator namespace describe default` readiness probe the workflow uses — and Task 4 lints the workflow before it ever reaches CI. Both negative cases for AC #2 (env unset → panic; server unreachable → connect failure) are locally checkable too, so no throwaway CI commit is needed.

**Task 3 has a gate that can *fail*, not just print.** Steps 6–7 only prove the script emits the right strings. Step 9 sets `AGENTCORE_COLD_START_LIMIT_MS=1` and requires exit 1, and Step 8 sets `AGENTCORE_SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES=1` and requires the variable to be *inert* — that's the assertion that the STOP RULE has no env escape hatch.

The task ordering is deliberate on cost: Task 2's Dockerfile work warms the Docker cache, so Task 3's four full script runs are cheap rather than four cold musl builds.

---

### Stage 4 — execution mode

**Subagent-driven** (`superpowers:subagent-driven-development`) — fresh subagent per task with review between. Seven tasks spanning Rust, bash, Dockerfile, YAML, and docs is well past the "1–2 tasks, single tightly-scoped area" bar for inline execution.

One caveat I'll manage: per a recorded lesson from SMA-452, implementer subagents tend to background long `cargo`/`docker` runs and end their turn mid-task. Tasks 1, 2, 3, and 7 all contain multi-minute builds, so every dispatch will carry an explicit instruction to work synchronously in the foreground and not finish until the command reaches a terminal status.

Say the word and I'll start Task 1 — or tell me to run it inline instead.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot

    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];

    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process


## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

Fix round 1 of 5 on Task 4. The review found one Important defect in the workflow you created. It originated in the brief's YAML, not in your transcription — your transcription was verified byte-identical and correct. The plan has now been corrected; please apply the same fix to the file.

OPEN FINDING (Important) — `.github/workflows/integration.yml`, the `concurrency:` block:

The group key omits `github.event_name`. This workflow triggers on `push` to main, `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch` — all three resolve `github.ref` to `refs/heads/main`, so they share one concurrency group. With `cancel-in-progress: false` for non-PR events, a queued run in a shared group is silently replaced rather than protected: if the 05:00 cron queues behind an in-progress push run and a second merge lands, that second push cancels the queued cron run. The nightly never executes, leaving no red status anywhere — and per this file's own header comment, the nightly cron is what accumulates the flake record the promotion decision depends on.

This repo already diagnosed and fixed this exact bug class in SMA-479. See `.github/workflows/audit.yml:19` and `.github/workflows/deny.yml:16`, and the CLAUDE.md CI section, which says of that key: "This is load-bearing, not decoration ... Do not simplify the key back."

REQUIRED CHANGE — replace the `concurrency:` block with exactly this (comment included; it is load-bearing documentation):

```yaml
concurrency:
  # Keyed on github.event_name as well as github.ref — load-bearing, not
  # decoration, and the same rule CLAUDE.md records for audit.yml/deny.yml.
  # push-to-main, schedule, and workflow_dispatch all resolve github.ref to
  # refs/heads/main, so a shared group with cancel-in-progress: false would let a
  # queued nightly sit pending until the next merge cancels it — silently
  # discarding the flake record this workflow exists to accumulate. Do not
  # simplify the key back.
  group: integration-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}-${{ github.event_name }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
```

Change nothing else in the file. In particular do NOT touch the "Self-test the never-green-by-skip guard" step's `if:` — a separate Minor finding about it was reviewed and deliberately rejected; the current behaviour is correct.

Closes [SMA-457](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-457/ci-add-temporal-it-and-agentcore-docker-build-jobs).

SMA-332 shipped two validation suites as local-only by GATE 1 decision, and CI has never executed either. This wires both in as **signal-only** (non-required) jobs.

## What lands

**New `.github/workflows/integration.yml`** with two jobs:

- **`temporal-it`** — installs a checksum-pinned `temporalio/cli` v1.8.2 tarball, runs `temporal server start-dev --headless`, and executes all six `temporal_live` tests. Path-filtered to the Temporal crate + core. Runs on PR, push to `main`, a nightly cron, and `workflow_dispatch`.
- **`agentcore-image`** — builds both AgentCore container images natively on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` and runs the four gates from `scripts/agentcore-image-check.sh`. Narrow path filter; opts out of the nightly.

## The bug this ticket nearly shipped with

`gate()` in `temporal_live.rs` prints `SKIPPED:` and **returns** — which means the test *passes*. `cargo test` captures a passing test's output, so the string is never printed. A CI job running that suite would have been green whether or not it ever reached a Temporal server: a typo'd env var, an `env:` on the wrong step, or a server that died after the readiness poll would all look identical to a clean run. That is the exact "compiles but never executes" weakness this ticket exists to remove, with a green checkmark on top.

Fixed with a `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL=1` guard that turns the silent skip into a panic — following the existing `HELIKON_REQUIRE_SANDBOX` idiom (`os_sandbox.rs:21`), which `ci.yml` already uses with the comment *"never green-by-skip"*. The job sets it, and a dedicated self-test step runs the suite once with the server address withheld and **fails the job if it passes**, so deleting the guard can't silently restore the old behaviour.

## Design decisions worth flagging

**Not in `ci.yml`, deliberately.** `temporal-it` is *expected* to flake while it earns promotion — its crash-resume test aborts a real worker against wall-clock activity timeouts. A failing job makes its whole workflow run conclude `failure` whether or not it's required, so co-locating it would make "ci is red on `main`" meaningless. The separate workflow also hosts the nightly cron that accumulates the flake record.

**No retry loop**, unlike `sessions-it`'s 3×. `sessions-it` is required, so a flake there blocks a merge; this job is signal-only precisely to *measure* the flake rate, and a retry would erase that evidence. Promotion bar: ≥20 executed runs with ≤1 flake, or 30 consecutive green nightlies.

**The cold-start gate is overridable; the size gate is not.** CI sets `AGENTCORE_COLD_START_LIMIT_MS=250` because the 50 ms AC was measured on a quiet dev machine and a shared runner is a different instrument — the script prints a loud `NOTE: … this is NOT the AC value` whenever it differs from the default. The 30 MB size gate stays hardcoded: it carries the STOP RULE, and an env knob there would be the quiet relaxation that rule exists to prevent. `AGENTCORE_SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES` is inert by design, and that's asserted.

**Neither job is added to `main-protection-checks.json`**, and neither uses `continue-on-error` — that would report green unconditionally, removing the signal rather than weakening it.

**PR title is `ci(...)` on purpose.** It touches files under two crates, and release-plz attributes bumps by path; `ci` carries `increment: None` in `.versionrc`, so nothing gets bumped for a CI-only change.

## Supporting changes

- `Dockerfile`: BuildKit cache mounts so the second image reuses the first's compiled deps. Measured locally at **96.4s → 18.8s** (~81%). The `cp` out of `target/` must stay inside that `RUN` — a cache mount isn't part of the image filesystem — and the file says so.
- `agentcore-image-check.sh`: the override above, `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1`, and a `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` block emitted *before* the gate checks so a failing run still records its numbers.

## Testing

Every CI gate from CLAUDE.md, locally: `fmt`, `clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings`, `test --workspace --all-features` (**1307 passed / 0 failed**), `doc` with `-D warnings`, and doc-coverage (**100%**, threshold 80). `mdbook build docs/book` clean. `actionlint` clean on the new workflow.

Beyond the gates:

- The full six-test Temporal suite run against a **real local dev server** — 6 passed in 21.97s — using the same `operator namespace describe default` readiness probe the workflow uses.
- Both negative paths: env unset → guard panics; `TEMPORAL_TEST_SERVER=127.0.0.1:79` → `connect()` fails.
- Four runs of the image-check script: default (no NOTE, `< 30 MB` / `< 50 ms`, exit 0), override to 250 (NOTE shown, exit 0), `AGENTCORE_SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES=1` (inert — STOP RULE has no escape hatch), and override to 1 (**exit 1**, proving it still gates rather than merely printing).
- Local image measurements after the Dockerfile change: echo 1.33 MB, agent 3.30 MB, cold starts 13 ms / 11 ms — binary confirmed present via `docker export | tar -t`.

The first CI run is itself the remaining test: it must show `6 passed` with no `SKIPPED:`, the guard self-test printing `guard OK`, and the arm64 job reporting all four gates. The observed CI cold-start and disk figures get recorded in the runbook as a follow-up commit on this branch.

## Docs

`CLAUDE.md` (new `integration.yml` section, plus a pre-existing `build-no-default-features` drift fixed in passing), `CONTRIBUTING.md` (line 242's "Live tests are not part of CI" is no longer true), the AgentCore runbook (override, BuildKit requirement, corrected disk prerequisite + `docker builder prune`), the Temporal README, and one clause in `docs/book/src/concepts/runtimes.md` where "the 50 ms gate" became ambiguous once two budgets exist.

Design and plan: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-sma-457-ci-integration-jobs-design.md`, `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-07-sma-457-ci-integration-jobs.md`.

## Important

### I1. The entire cold Rust compile happens inside a step capped at 20 minutes
`.github/workflows/integration.yml:159`

Step order in `temporal-it` is: checkout → filter → decide → toolchain → protoc → rust-cache → install CLI → start server → **run suite (`timeout-minutes: 20`)**. Nothing compiles before the suite step, so `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal --test temporal_live` inside that step must build the crate's full dependency closure — 259 packages (`cargo tree --no-dedupe | sort -u | wc -l`), including `aws-lc-rs` (cmake + C/asm), `prost-build`/`tonic-build`/`tonic-prost-build` running protoc codegen over Temporal's proto set, and `temporalio-sdk-core`/`-client`/`-common`/`-workflow`.

This directly contradicts the spec's own reasoning: §5 justifies `timeout-minutes: 60` at *job* level because "the same budget must absorb a from-scratch build of `temporalio-sdk-core` … the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace", and §5 also states the implementing PR "runs with a guaranteed cold cache". The 60-minute budget is unreachable — the only compiling step is capped at 20.

Failure scenario: first CI run on this PR (cold cache by construction). Compile takes >20 min → GitHub kills the step → `steps.suite.outcome == 'failure'`. Three consequences, in ascending badness: (a) the job goes red for a reason unrelated to Temporal; (b) the "Dump the dev-server log" step fires and prints a perfectly healthy server log, misdirecting triage; (c) the summary step writes `outcome: **failure**` into the flake record — indistinguishable from a genuine `crash_resume_mid_tool_call` flake. The job exists to produce a trustworthy flake record and this poisons the first data point.

Fix (one step): insert `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal --test temporal_live --no-run` before the "Start the Temporal dev server" step, leaving `timeout-minutes: 20` to cover execution only. Bonus: a compile error then fails before the CLI install/server start, and the dev server no longer idles for 20 minutes. Alternative: raise the step cap to ~45 and rely on the job's 60.

### I2. The AgentCore crate README's `docker build` commands now require BuildKit and don't say so
`crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore/README.md:110-124`

The Dockerfile gained `RUN --mount=type=cache` (`docker/Dockerfile:79-80`). The runbook was updated ("Docker with BuildKit — now mandatory, not merely default"), and the check script exports `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` — but the crate README, which is this crate's crates.io and docs.rs landing page, still presents both `docker build …` commands verbatim with no BuildKit prerequisite, and those commands do **not** go through the script.

Failure scenario: a downstream consumer on Docker < 23, or with `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0` exported (the exact stale-environment case the script's own comment calls out), copy-pastes the README block and gets `dockerfile parse error line 79: Unknown flag: mount` — with nothing in the README pointing at the cause.

This is also a convention miss: spec §7's docs table lists five files and omits this README, and CLAUDE.md requires "update the affected crate's README in the same PR as any change to … its install or feature story". One sentence above the fenced block fixes it.

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-sma-457-ci-integration-jobs-design.md:521-525`

The spec asserts: *"`ci` carries `increment: None` in `.versionrc`, so a `ci(...)`-titled PR bumps nothing."* That conflates two different tools. `.versionrc` is **convco's** config — it drives the `commits` gate and the local `commit-msg` hook. release-plz does not read it; it uses its own `next_version` logic (feat → minor, breaking → major, **everything else → patch**) and attributes changes by file path.

Empirical proof from this repo's own history: `6ebac2c docs(repo): SMA-424 refresh crate READMEs to match the shipped surface (#93)` changed only `crates/*/README.md`. The next commit, `b0671ec chore: release (#94)`, bumped and published **nine** crates — e.g. `paigasus-helikon-core` `0.5.4 → 0.5.5` with a `### Other — *(repo)* SMA-424 refresh crate READMEs …` changelog entry. `docs` also carries `increment: None` in `.versionrc`.

This is harmless in itself (patch republish, no library-code change), but it is the opposite of what the spec promises, and the spec lands on `main` as a durable artifact. Fix the §8 bullet to say "expect a release PR bumping runtime-temporal, runtime-agentcore, and the facade; the `ci` type only keeps it out of the *changelog highlights*, it does not suppress the bump", and expect to review that bot PR post-merge.

### I4. Both disk-reporting steps abort the job on a tool hiccup — and the post-build one can flip a fully-passing gate run to red
`.github/workflows/integration.yml:265-280` and `:292-302`

*(This is the ledger's flagged item; I'm raising it above "minor" because of the second half.)*

Both run under the default `bash -e {0}`, and `set -e` applies inside the `{ … } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"` compound. `docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'` (line 278) and `docker system df` (line 300) both require a reachable daemon.

Same class as I2 but lower severity (the reader is already in the file). The two documented `docker build` invocations sit at lines 9-19; the BuildKit requirement is stated at lines 68-71, ~60 lines below, inside the `RUN` block's comment. A one-line note next to the commands would close it.

What will actually happen on merge: the squashed `ci(workflows): …` commit touches `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal/{README.md,tests/temporal_live.rs}` and `crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore/docker/Dockerfile` (all three are inside the packaged tarballs), so release-plz opens a `chore: release` PR bumping `paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal` `0.2.2 → 0.2.3` and `paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore` `0.2.0 → 0.2.1`, and — via `dependencies_update = true` and the facade's optional deps at `crates/paigasus-helikon/Cargo.toml:24-25` — cascading a patch bump to `paigasus-helikon`.

This is harmless in itself (patch republish, no library-code change), but it is the opposite of what the spec promises, and the spec lands on `main` as a durable artifact. Fix the §8 bullet to say "expect a release PR bumping runtime-temporal, runtime-agentcore, and the facade; the `ci` type only keeps it out of the *changelog highlights*, it does not suppress the bump", and expect to review that bot PR post-merge.

### I4. Both disk-reporting steps abort the job on a tool hiccup — and the post-build one can flip a fully-passing gate run to red
`.github/workflows/integration.yml:265-280` and `:292-302`

*(This is the ledger's flagged item; I'm raising it above "minor" because of the second half.)*

Both run under the default `bash -e {0}`, and `set -e` applies inside the `{ … } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"` compound. `docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'` (line 278) and `docker system df` (line 300) both require a reachable daemon.

- Pre-build (`:265`): a failure aborts before the build, so the job is red having measured nothing, and the summary is left with an unterminated code fence.
- Post-build (`:292`): this one is guarded by `always() && …`, so it runs *after a successful build*. If `docker system df` fails there, **all four gates passed and the job still reports red.** For a job whose credibility rests on not going red for unrelated reasons, that is the wrong way round.

Likelihood is low (Docker is up on GitHub-hosted runners) but the fix is one token: `|| true` on the two `docker` lines, or `set +e` at the top of each reporting step.

---

## Minor

### M1. The `build-no-default-features` "the crate" drift is now three-way asymmetric, not two-way
`CLAUDE.md:111`, `CONTRIBUTING.md:298`

The ledger spotted `CONTRIBUTING.md:298`. It missed that **`CLAUDE.md:111`** — the required-status-check contexts paragraph, a different sentence from the one the branch fixed at `CLAUDE.md:97` — also still reads *"the only gate that compiles the crate with default features off"* (singular). So the branch corrected one of three sites. Since it chose to fix the drift, leaving two stale is worse than leaving all three: a reader now has one correct and two incorrect statements with no way to tell which is current. Two one-line edits ("both `runtime-axum` and `runtime-actix`").

### M2. Filter-miss message is wrong on `schedule` for `agentcore-image`
`.github/workflows/integration.yml:263-264`

`echo "No AgentCore image-related changes; nothing to run."` fires on the nightly too, where `decide` mapped `schedule → false` deliberately (line 256-257) and no filter ran at all. Anyone triaging "why did the nightly produce no image measurement?" reads a message that says the opposite of the truth. Fix: branch the message on `github.event_name == 'schedule'`.

### M3. Dockerfile header's copy-pasteable build commands lack the BuildKit note
`crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore/docker/Dockerfile:9-19`

Same class as I2 but lower severity (the reader is already in the file). The two documented `docker build` invocations sit at lines 9-19; the BuildKit requirement is stated at lines 68-71, ~60 lines below, inside the `RUN` block's comment. A one-line note next to the commands would close it.

### M4. Job-summary duration is blank when the suite step times out
`.github/workflows/integration.yml:197,205`

`duration_s` is written at `:175`, after `cargo test` returns. If the step is killed by `timeout-minutes` (see I1), `GITHUB_OUTPUT` is never written and the summary renders `- suite wall-clock: s`. Cosmetic, but it degrades exactly the record the job exists to produce, and it co-occurs with the most likely failure mode.

### M5–M8 — carried from the ledger, see the triage table below.

---

## Things I checked and found correct (not findings)

- **No check-run name collision.** Job ids across all workflows are unique; `temporal-it`/`agentcore-image` collide with nothing in `ci.yml` (`fmt`, `clippy`, `test`, `build-no-default-features`, `docs`, `doc-coverage`, `commits`, `sessions-it`).
- **No concurrency-group collision.** Every workflow prefixes its group with its own name; `integration-…-${{ github.event_name }}` correctly follows the `audit.yml`/`deny.yml` rule CLAUDE.md calls load-bearing (fixed in `edd3f9e` after Task 4's review).
- **`ci.yml`'s required contexts are unaffected.** `.github/rulesets/main-protection-checks.json` is untouched (AC 7 ✓); adding a workflow does not make its contexts required. `ci.yml`'s "eight jobs" sentence stays correct because both jobs live elsewhere.
- **`ci.yml`'s `test` job does not set `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL`**, so the live suite still loud-skips there — the local contract (AC 3) is genuinely unchanged.
- **The `decide` pattern is sound across all four triggers plus filter-miss.** `${MATCHED:-false}` correctly handles the skipped-filter empty output; `schedule`/`workflow_dispatch` short-circuit before ever reading it; step-level (not job-level) guards mean both jobs always report a status.
- **Adversarial misleading-green check on `temporal-it`: clean, and stronger than advertised.** A renamed test target errors; an unset `TEMPORAL_TEST_SERVER` panics via the guard; a dead server panics in `connect()`. Notably, the self-test at `:177` *also* catches the case where someone blanket-`#[ignore]`s the suite (`0 passed` exits 0 → `if cargo test` succeeds → the step errors). That's an unclaimed benefit.
- **The self-test is genuinely cheap.** `HELIKON_REQUIRE_TEMPORAL` and `TEMPORAL_TEST_SERVER` are read with `std::env::var` at runtime, not `env!()`, so removing one between steps triggers no rebuild.
- **Script exit-code propagation is correct** despite `exit 1` living inside a command substitution (`echo_cold_start_ms=$(measure_cold_start_ms …)`): the subshell's non-zero status becomes the assignment's status, and `set -e` aborts. `SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES` has no env escape hatch (grep: `AGENTCORE_SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES` appears nowhere in the script), so the STOP RULE holds — the runbook's "inert" claim is accurate.
- **Conventions honoured:** all five actions SHA-pinned to the exact pins already in `ci.yml` with matching `# action vX.Y.Z` comments; no new third-party action; every commit scope (`spec`, `plan`, `runtime-temporal`, `runtime-agentcore`, `workflows`, `claude`) is in `.versionrc`'s `scopeRegex`; the PR title's `workflows` scope is in `pr-title.yml`'s allowlist and the subject starts lowercase; branch name matches the `feature/**` ruleset; no workspace-inheritance or per-crate-version rules touched.
- **Doc sweep for stale `50 ms` claims: clean.** Every surviving `< 50 ms` is in a table recording the macOS validated run, where 50 ms genuinely *was* the effective gate.

---

## Ledger triage

|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Panic message lacks the remediation hint the sibling `eprintln!` carries | **Defer** | Matches the `HELIKON_REQUIRE_SANDBOX` precedent's terseness; the message names both env vars, so the fix is discoverable. |
| T2 | Dockerfile comment says "roughly 40-50%", measured 81% | **Defer** | Conservative, never overpromises. Note it is now repeated at `CLAUDE.md:105` — if it's ever corrected, correct both. |

Adding `always() &&` would buy nothing and cost a rebuild-check on every red run. |
| T5a | **"Report runner capacity" has no `always()`/failure tolerance — flagged for final triage** | **Fix first — see I4.** Upgraded from Minor: the *sibling* step at `:292` is the sharper edge, because it carries `always()` and therefore runs after a **successful** build, so a `docker system df` failure turns a fully-passing gate run red. Fix both, not just the one the ledger names. |

**Outstanding spec deliverable (not a defect, but not done):** spec §6.4 and §7 both require the runbook to record "the first observed CI figure alongside the macOS row", and §6.3 requires the disk measurement to be acted on. That is plan Task 7 Step 5, still open — the branch head `6b9cd4f` has no CI row in `docs/runbooks/agentcore-image-check.md`. AC 4 and AC 9 are likewise unverifiable until the first real run.

---

## Verdict: **fix first**

Nothing here is a correctness hole in what the branch measures — the never-green-by-skip guard is sound, the gates genuinely gate, and the workflow's decide/guard mechanics are correct across all four triggers. But four items should land before merge:

1. **I1** — move the cold compile out of the 20-minute-capped step. This is the one most likely to bite on the very first run, and it corrupts the flake record rather than merely annoying.
2. **I4 / T5a** — two `|| true`s, so a successful gate run cannot report red.
3. **I2** — one sentence in the AgentCore crate README.
4. **I3** — correct spec §8's release claim, and expect a `chore: release` PR bumping two crates plus the facade after merge.

M1, M2 and the T5b message are cheap enough to fold into the same pass. Everything else in the ledger is correctly deferred.

### F2 — `.github/workflows/integration.yml`: disk-report steps must not fail the job

### F3 — `.github/workflows/integration.yml`: capacity/disk figures must reach the job log, not only the summary

```yaml
          if [ "${EVENT}" = "schedule" ]; then

          else
            echo "No AgentCore image-related changes; nothing to run."
          fi
```

Find the actual section — do not guess its location.

The file's header documents two copy-pasteable `docker build` invocations near the top, while the BuildKit requirement is explained ~60 lines below inside the builder `RUN`'s comment. Add a one-line note next to those header commands.

An earlier task corrected the description at `CLAUDE.md:97` but two other sites still describe that job as compiling "**the crate**" (singular), when it now builds both `runtime-axum` and `runtime-actix` plus a `cargo tree` axum-leakage assertion (see `.github/workflows/ci.yml`). - `CLAUDE.md:111` (the required-status-check contexts paragraph — a *different* sentence from the one already fixed at :97)
- `CONTRIBUTING.md:298` (the repo-configuration table row)
Read `ci.yml` first and describe what the job actually does. Keep each edit to a clause.

### F8 — `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-sma-457-ci-integration-jobs-design.md` §8: the release-plz claim is wrong

The "Release impact" bullet claims: *"`ci` carries `increment: None` in `.versionrc`, so a `ci(...)`-titled PR bumps nothing."* That conflates two tools. `.versionrc` is **convco's** config — it drives the `commits` CI gate and the local `commit-msg` hook. release-plz does not read it; it has its own logic (feat → minor, breaking → major, **everything else → patch**) and attributes changes by file path.

### Added

- *(runtime-temporal)* SMA-462 replace positional activity inputs with a versionable envelope ([#176](https://github.com/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon/pull/176))

### Changed

- *(runtime-temporal)* SMA-462 activity inputs are now a **single self-describing envelope payload**
  - `render_instructions`, `call_model` and `invoke_tool` each take one JSON-object payload instead of positional arguments. Workers on this version also decode the previous pre-envelope positional shapes from 0.2.0 or 0.2.1 specifically, so activity tasks queued by a worker on either of those two versions execute normally. 0.1.x is outside the support window: its `render_instructions` and `invoke_tool` shapes fail closed with a decode error rather than being silently misread.
  - No public Rust API change — the envelope types are crate-internal.
  - Future additive changes to an activity's input are now compatible in both directions (unknown fields ignored, absent fields defaulted). This is scoped to the envelope's own field set: it does **not** cover the `paigasus-helikon-core` types nested inside them (`ModelRequest`, `ToolCallRequest`) or activity outputs.

### Upgrade notes

- **Upgrade one release at a time**, and keep the mixed-fleet window short. A 0.2.1-and-earlier worker handed one of the new envelope payloads cannot decode it; it fails the attempt retryably and Temporal re-dispatches until a worker on this version takes it. Four things bound that recovery: a finite `maximum_attempts` on `model_retry_policy` / `tool_retry_policy` can be exhausted; `WorkflowInput::timeout_ms` interrupts the run regardless of retry policy; a terminal `render_instructions` failure ends the run outright; and exhausted `invoke_tool` retries are folded into a tool-error result fed to the model rather than failing loudly.
- **Prefer draining in-flight runs before this upgrade**, or ensure retry caps are unlimited and run deadlines generous for the duration of the rollout. Blue-green task queues remain available.
- **Rolling back requires a drain.** Once a worker on this version has queued an envelope-shaped activity task, that payload is frozen in the `ActivityTaskScheduled` event and every retry re-delivers it; a rollback to 0.2.1 and earlier leaves those activities undecodable until the run deadline.
- Activity input encoding is **not** a replay hazard: Temporal's replay check compares an activity's id and type only, never its input payloads. Verified against `temporalio-* = 0.5.0`; re-verify on any SDK bump.

lines: ## Global Constraints

- **Commit format:** `<type>(<scope>): SMA-457 <lowercase message>`. Allowed scopes are in `.versionrc`; this plan uses `ci`, `workflows`, `runtime-temporal`, `runtime-agentcore`, `docs`, `claude`, `contributing`, `readme`, `plan`. A local `commit-msg` hook runs `convco check` and will reject anything else.

-- **PR title must be `ci(...)` or `ci(workflows): ...`** — never `feat`/`fix`. `ci` carries `increment: None` in `.versionrc`, so release-plz attributes no version bump. A `feat`/`fix` title would bump `runtime-temporal` and `runtime-agentcore` for a CI-only change.

+- **PR title must be `ci(...)` or `ci(workflows): ...`** — never `feat`/`fix`. Note what this does and does not buy: `.versionrc`'s `increment: None` for `ci` governs **convco** (the `commits` gate and the local hook), *not* release-plz. release-plz has its own logic and attributes by file path, so it will still open a `chore: release` PR patch-bumping `runtime-temporal` and `runtime-agentcore` — every crate here is 0.x, where feat also maps to patch. The `ci` type therefore changes the changelog section, not the bump.
- **Never `git add -A`** — `.env` and `.claude` are untracked but not gitignored. Stage explicit paths and verify with `git show --stat`.
- **Never move HEAD or switch branches.** This worktree is shared with other sessions.

- **Reuse the action SHAs already pinned in `ci.yml`.** Do not look up newer ones: Dependabot's `github-actions` group bumps all occurrences together, and introducing a second pin for the same action fragments that. The exact pins are listed in Task 4.

## Implementation complete — PR [#181](https://github.com/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon/pull/181)

## Three things the process caught that I'd otherwise have shipped

**The spec-challenger found a blocker that defeated the ticket.** `gate()` returns `None` → the test *passes*, and `cargo test` swallows a passing test's output. My acceptance criterion ("zero `SKIPPED:` lines") was unfalsifiable — a job that never reached a server would have been indistinguishable from a green one.

**A task review caught me violating a documented CLAUDE.md rule.** My concurrency group omitted `github.event_name`. Since `push`/`schedule`/`workflow_dispatch` all resolve `github.ref` to `refs/heads/main`, a queued nightly could be silently cancelled by the next merge — destroying the exact flake record the workflow exists to collect. CLAUDE.md says of that key: *"Do not simplify the key back."*

**The scoped re-review caught the fix wave introducing a *new* falsehood.** Correcting my wrong release-plz claim, the fixer wrote "feat → minor, breaking → major" — inverted for 0.x crates. Confirmed against this repo's own changelog: `runtime-temporal` 0.2.1 → **0.2.2** came from an `### Added` entry, a patch bump.

## One finding I rejected, with data

The final review's top item predicted the cold Rust compile would blow the 20-minute step cap. The run disproved it: rust-cache logged **"No cache found."** — genuinely cold, the exact worst case — and the compile took **~140s against a 1200s cap**. Sound reasoning, wrong premise. No change made.

## Two things you should know

**A `chore: release` PR *will* open on merge, contrary to what I told you at GATE 1.** I claimed the `ci` title meant no version bump. That was wrong — `.versionrc` is convco's config; release-plz doesn't read it and attributes by file path. Expect patch bumps to `runtime-temporal`, `runtime-agentcore`, and a cascaded facade bump. Harmless (no library code changed), but watch that bot PR's CI.

**The nightly opt-out's justification was wrong, so you may want to revisit it.** I estimated the arm64 double-build at 40–60 minutes; it's **4 minutes**. I corrected the figure everywhere but deliberately did *not* flip the decision — that's yours. At 4 minutes a nightly would be cheap, though the honest argument for skipping it still holds: re-measuring two numbers sitting at ~9% and ~23% of budget adds no information.
